pages.name: Fifty readings
pages.text: It starts at the true value, 0.80 Ω. Twelve pegs each nudge it a little left or right on the way down. In this simulation, many small causes add up like that. Fifty readings gather round the middle. The beam balances on its fulcrum at the mean. That is all the readings added up and divided by how many. The dotted line is one bead's path through the pegs.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated readings fall through a field of pegs, land on a beam marked in ohms and rise into a swarm, balanced on a fulcrum at their mean.

pages.name: Where it balances
pages.task: Five readings sit on the beam: 0.79, 0.80, 0.80, 0.81 and 0.85 Ω. Where does it balance?
pages.why: They add to 4.05 Ω, and 4.05 ÷ 5 = 0.81 Ω. Below 0.81 sit 0.02 + 0.01 + 0.01 = 0.04 Ω of distance. Above it sits 0.04 Ω too, so the beam balances there.

pages.name: A slipped probe
pages.text: Put the readings in order and the middle one is the median. A dotted line marks it. Here a probe has slipped on the ringed reading, making it 1.80 Ω, off the end of the scale. That adds 1.00 Ω to the total. So the mean has crept up a fiftieth of it, 0.02 Ω, and the fulcrum with it. The median has barely moved. The slipped reading only jumped to the top of the order.

pages.name: Mean or median
pages.task: Nine readings of a circuit say 0.50 Ω. A tenth, taken with a slipped probe, says 1.50 Ω. What are the mean and the median?
pages.why: The ten add to 4.50 + 1.50 = 6.00 Ω, so the mean is 0.60 Ω. The slip lifted it by 1.00 ÷ 10 = 0.10 Ω. In order, the fifth and sixth readings are both 0.50 Ω, so the median stays 0.50 Ω.

pages.name: Spread by a factor
pages.text: These readings scatter round 200 MΩ. Here each nudge makes a reading bigger or smaller by a factor, not by a fixed amount. On a scale where each column is 12% more than the last, the swarm is a bell. On an even scale it leans. Most readings bunch low and a few run far high. That long tail pulls the mean above the median. So the beam balances to the right of the median. When a swarm leans like this, the mean alone can mislead.

pages.name: Halve the random error
pages.text: Halving the random error from 0.02 Ω to 0.01 Ω halves each bead's twelve jinks through the pegs. So the swarm is half as wide and nearly twice as tall. The pegs move up to clear it. It is only nearly twice, because the meter rounds each reading to 0.01 Ω. The fulcrum stays at very nearly 0.80 Ω. So the mean alone cannot tell a steady reading from a jumpy one. The spread needs a number of its own.
pages.alt: The swarm of fifty readings under its field of pegs, balanced on its fulcrum. The random error sets how far the pegs spread.

pages.name: Same range
pages.task: Set A is 0.76, 0.80, 0.80, 0.80 and 0.84 Ω. Set B is 0.76, 0.76, 0.80, 0.84 and 0.84 Ω. Both have a mean of 0.80 Ω. The range is the highest reading minus the lowest. Both ranges are 0.08 Ω. Which is more spread out?
pages.answer: B: more of its readings sit far out
pages.why: In A, three of the five readings sit right on the mean. In B, four sit 0.04 Ω away from it. So B is more spread out, though both ranges are 0.08 Ω. The range uses only the two end readings.

pages.name: The standard deviation
pages.text: The [[standard deviation]], or SD, is how far readings typically sit from the mean. These five have a mean of 0.80 Ω. Each bead rises to show its distance from it. Square each distance, so the minus signs go. Then finish as for an AC RMS, with one change. Add the squares and divide by one fewer than the count, here 4. Readings sit a little closer to their own mean than to the true value. Dividing by one fewer makes up for that. The root is the SD, 0.02 Ω.

pages.task: Two sets of ten both have a mean of 0.80 Ω. A has three beads at 0.78, four at 0.80 and three at 0.82 Ω. B has one in each column from 0.75 to 0.85 Ω, with 0.80 empty. Which has the larger standard deviation?
pages.why: Every reading in A sits within 0.02 Ω of the mean. B's reach out to 0.05 Ω. So B's SD, about 0.035 Ω, is about twice A's, about 0.016 Ω. Bumps in the column heights do not count.

pages.name: Two testers
pages.task: Two testers each read one circuit ten times. A gets a mean of 0.80 Ω and an SD of 0.01 Ω. B gets a mean of 0.80 Ω and an SD of 0.04 Ω. What does that say?
pages.answer: B's readings sit about four times as far out
pages.why: The mean says where readings centre, and both centre on 0.80 Ω. The SD says how far they typically sit from it. B's 0.04 Ω is four times A's 0.01 Ω, so B's readings wobble about four times as much.

pages.name: Twelve sockets
pages.task: You read Zs once at each of twelve sockets, all on different circuits. The mean is 0.65 Ω and the SD is 0.18 Ω. What does the 0.18 Ω mostly tell you?
pages.why: Each reading comes from a different circuit. So their spread is mostly how the circuits differ, plus a little wobble of the reading. To judge how far to trust one reading, read one circuit several times.
